## Arrow Impossibility Theorem

The solution to the vehicle problem can be viewed as a social choice problem.
For example, scooters by small children might be acceptable, but powered scooters
would be unacceptable.  The optimal decision is a function of the preferences
of the individuals using the park.

For example, suppose that only power scooters and bicycles use the park, in
which case the goal is to stop cars.  However, if only the pedestrians use the
park, then the goal is to stop powered vehicles.  The point this is that the
optimal depends upon the preferences of individuals using the park.  This the
optimal decision is not simply the literal rule, but also the preferences of the
individuals using the park.

However, we know that no social choice mechanism can perfectly aggregate
individual preferences into a collective decision that satisfies all desirable
criteria, as demonstrated by Arrow's Impossibility Theorem.

This implies that any attempt to design an AI system that aligns with human
values must confront the inherent limitations of aggregating diverse
preferences.  In other words, the AI alignment problem cannot be fully solved
because there is no mechanism that can perfectly reconcile all individual
preferences into a single, optimal decision. 

Since the optimal choice is a function of individuals to whom the AI has no
contact with, it is not possible for the AI to make a fully optimal decision that accounts for all individual preferences.  This limitation is inherent and cannot be overcome by any algorithmic design.  

In the legal context the decision problem is solved (imperfectly) by having a court
case where parties present information, and then the judge decides.  This illustrates that
that "human values" are not represented by an axiomatic system, but the explicit
consequence of a human judge and jury deliberating over the case.  This highlights the contrast with AI systems, which lack the ability to engage in such deliberative processes and therefore cannot fully capture the nuances of human values.

This is a fairly complete paper.  The idea of using the hopfield network to think about AI design would be a new paper.  It could speak to optimal AI intelligence in the context
of performance design. 

Notes from Janet.

Asks why adding judge makes a difference.  My response it that judge searches a different
part of the database.  The judge brings in additional context and reasoning that the AI might not have access to, thereby influencing the final decision in a way that purely algorithmic processing cannot replicate.  Janet argues that one solution to the arrow problem is the use of lexigraphical preferences.  This approach prioritizes certain preferences over others in a hierarchical manner, potentially circumventing some of the limitations imposed by Arrow's theorem.
